> **How to read this file.** Section 3 runs the simulation, sections 4 and 5 show the evidence, and section 8 states my selected n. The reusable code lives in `R/functions.R`; this file only calls it.

## 1. Prediction

A fair die is perfectly symmetric, so I predict skewness stays near 0 at every n. But every face is equally likely, so it has lighter tails than a normal curve (negative excess kurtosis). I predict that kurtosis is the check that holds it back at small n, that it shrinks toward 0 as n grows, and that the die reaches "approximately normal" at a very small n, such as 4.

## 2. The population

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/setup.R")
source("R/functions.R")

generator <- function(n) sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE)
mu    <- 3.5
sigma <- sqrt(35 / 12)
kappa <- -6 * (6^2 + 1) / (5 * (6^2 - 1))
```

Six-sided die: each face 1 to 6 has probability 1/6.

- Mean: μ = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = `r mu`.
- Standard deviation: σ = √(35/12) = `r round(sigma, 3)`, so the theoretical standard error of the mean is σ/√n.
- Shape: perfectly symmetric (skewness 0), but flat-topped. Its excess kurtosis is −6(6² + 1) / (5(6² − 1)) = `r round(kappa, 3)`. The excess kurtosis of an average of n independent rolls is this value divided by n, so I can compare my simulation with the theory kappa / n.

```{r}
#| label: population-plot
#| fig-height: 3
barplot(rep(1 / 6, 6), names.arg = 1:6, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
        ylim = c(0, 0.25), main = "Six-sided die population",
        xlab = "face", ylab = "probability")
```

## 3. Simulation

For every sample size n in my list (`r min(n_values)` to `r max(n_values)`, `r length(n_values)` sizes), I draw B = `r format(B, big.mark = ",")` samples of n rolls and keep each sample's mean. B is the number of repetitions; n is the size of each sample.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
all_means <- simulate_all_n(generator, n_values)
results   <- summarize_means(all_means, mu, sigma)
results$good <- flag_good(results)
n_star <- smallest_good_n(results)

dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(results, "results/02_die.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## 4. Results

Selected sample sizes (the full table of all `r nrow(results)` sizes is saved in `results/02_die.csv`). The column `theory_kurtosis` is the theoretical excess kurtosis, kappa / n:

```{r}
#| label: table
key_n <- sort(unique(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, n_star)))
show  <- results[results$n %in% key_n, c("n", "sim_mean", "theory_mean", "sim_sd",
                                         "theory_se", "sd_ratio", "skewness",
                                         "excess_kurtosis")]
show$theory_kurtosis <- kappa / show$n
show$passes <- ifelse(results$good[results$n %in% key_n], "yes", "no")
knitr::kable(show, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

## 5. Plots

**Histograms of the sample means**, with the theoretical normal curve N(μ, σ/√n) in red. I show the same sample sizes in every analysis (1, 2, 5, 30) plus my selected n. Because a die only produces whole numbers, `step = 1` lines the bars up with the values the sample mean can actually take:

```{r}
#| label: histograms
show_n <- sort(unique(c(1, 2, 5, 30, n_star)))
plot_histograms(all_means, show_n, mu, sigma, "Six-sided die", step = 1)
```

**Q–Q plots** (points on the red line = normal):

```{r}
#| label: qqplots
plot_qq(all_means, show_n, "Six-sided die")
```

These sample sizes are a sample of the picture: 1 is the raw population, 2 is the smallest amount of averaging, 5 is a small sample, 30 is the classic rule of thumb, and the last one is my selected n. Every n from 1 to 100 appears in the diagnostics chart below and in `results/02_die.csv`, and you can watch any n live in the **Interactive Sampling Distribution Explorer**

**Diagnostics across every n.** Dashed lines mark my "approximately normal" limits (defined in section 6):

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(results$n, results$skewness, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$skewness, -0.25, 0.25)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "skewness", main = "Skewness of sample means")
abline(h = c(-0.25, 0, 0.25), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")

plot(results$n, results$excess_kurtosis, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$excess_kurtosis, -0.5, 0.5)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "excess kurtosis", main = "Excess kurtosis")
abline(h = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")
lines(results$n, kappa / results$n, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

plot(results$n, results$sd_ratio, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$sd_ratio, 0.95, 1.05)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "simulated SD / theoretical SE", main = "Spread vs. theory")
abline(h = c(0.95, 1, 1.05), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")
```

In the middle chart, the blue line is the theoretical excess kurtosis (kappa / n); the black points are my simulation.

## 6. My definition of "approximately normal"

I use the same rule in every analysis. A sample size n counts as approximately normal when **all four** of these hold:

1.  The histogram is bell-shaped and the Q–Q plot is close to the line.
2.  \|skewness\| ≤ 0.25.
3.  \|excess kurtosis\| ≤ 0.5.
4.  The simulated SD is within 5% of the theoretical SE (σ/√n).

My selected n is the smallest n that passes and stays passing for every larger n I tested. The reasons for each cutoff are in [01_standard_normal.md](01_standard_normal.md).

## 7. Interpretation

```{r}
#| label: interpretation
at_star  <- results[results$n == n_star, ]
below    <- results[results$n == n_star - 1, ]
at_one   <- results[results$n == 1, ]
max_skew <- max(abs(results$skewness))
sd_lo    <- min(results$sd_ratio)
sd_hi    <- max(results$sd_ratio)
max_mean_err <- max(abs(results$sim_mean - results$theory_mean))
kurt_gap <- max(abs(results$excess_kurtosis - kappa / results$n))
```

- **Shape.** At n = 1 the histogram is six equal bars and the Q–Q plot is a staircase, because a single roll can only be 1 to 6. By n = 5 the bars form a bell and the steps in the Q–Q plot are small and follow the line; by n = 30 it looks practically straight.
- **Mean.** The simulated mean never differs from μ = 3.5 by more than `r round(max_mean_err, 3)`.
- **Spread.** The simulated SD divided by the theoretical SE stays between `r round(sd_lo, 3)` and `r round(sd_hi, 3)`, so the formula σ/√n holds at every n.
- **Skewness.** Skewness is symmetric by design: it stays within ±`r round(max_skew, 3)` at every n, which is just simulation noise.
- **Kurtosis decides it.** At n = 1 the excess kurtosis is `r round(at_one$excess_kurtosis, 3)` (theory `r round(kappa, 3)`), far outside my ±0.5 limit. It shrinks like kappa / n, and my simulated values follow that line apart from random noise (the largest gap is `r round(kurt_gap, 3)`, compared with a noise level of about ±`r round(sqrt(24 / B), 2)` per value). The kurtosis limit is first met at n = `r n_star`.

**CLT assumptions.** Rolls are independent and identically distributed, and a die has finite variance (it is bounded), so every assumption is met.

**Limitations / surprises.** The surprise is which check fails. The die has no skew, so the usual worry about a long tail does not apply. Instead it fails because it has too few extreme values (light tails), and averaging fixes that quickly. Also, because the die is discrete, the sample mean can only take certain values at small n, which is why the histograms and Q–Q plots look blocky there.

## 8. Selected n and justification

**Selected n = `r n_star`.**

- **Evidence at n = `r n_star`.** Skewness `r round(at_star$skewness, 3)` (limit ±0.25), excess kurtosis `r round(at_star$excess_kurtosis, 3)` (limit ±0.5), and SD ratio `r round(at_star$sd_ratio, 3)` (limit 1 ± 0.05). The histogram follows the normal curve, and the Q–Q plot follows the line apart from small steps caused by the die's discrete values.
- **Why not smaller.** At n = `r n_star - 1`, the excess kurtosis is `r round(below$excess_kurtosis, 3)`, outside my ±0.5 limit.
- **It stays passing.** Every larger n I tested, up to n = `r max(n_values)`, also passes.
- **Is the number 30?** No. The die needs only about n = `r n_star`, so 30 is roughly `r round(30 / n_star)` times more than necessary.
